title.title: The Ball–Evans approximation problem in three dimensions
title.subtitle: Claim: every $W^{1,p}$ homeomorphism between bounded domains in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is a limit of smooth diffeomorphisms

plain: Bend a rubber block without tearing: can perfectly smooth bendings copy it just as accurately?

beats.text: Schematic: a Sobolev homeomorphism $f$ deforms $\Omega$ onto $\Lambda$, like an elastic body
Smoothing it by convolution destroys injectivity
The plane was settled; dimension 4 and up has counterexamples; 3 was open

steps: Count how image curves cross a triangulation of the target
Rebuild the derivative patch by patch, keeping it one-to-one
Smooth the piecewise-linear result into a diffeomorphism

achievement.label: Ball-Evans approximation problem (Ball, 2001)
statement: f \in W^{1,p}(\Omega, \Lambda) \text{ homeo} \;\Rightarrow\; f_j \to f, \; f_j \text{ smooth diffeos}
achievement.context: Before: Hencl's 2025 survey called dimension 3 "wildly open"
achievement.note: Dimension 3 only; no claim about the inverses

verify.detail: No Lean: 192 pages of intricate geometric construction, the kind where gaps hide
verify.ourCheck: We reviewed the papers; we did not verify the constructions

voice.text: A Sobolev homeomorphism deforms a body like rubber. Convolution smoothing destroys injectivity.
Rebuild the map patch by patch against a triangulation, then smooth the whole result.
Claimed: settled in three dimensions, the open case.

sources.quote: Question attributed by J. Ball to L.C. Evans (Ball, 'Singularities and computation of minimizers', 2001).
Iwaniec–Kovalev–Onninen (p=2, ARMA 2011; then all 1<p<∞) and Hencl–Pratelli (p=1, JEMS 2018)
